content.title: How many masters has Tiger Woods won?
content.text: President Donald Trump has selected Erica Schwartz as his nominee to lead the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Schwartz, a career civil servant, served as deputy surgeon general during the first Trump administration and is considered an establishment pick for the role. “Erica graduated from Brown University for College and Medical School, and served a distinguished career as a Doctor of Medicine in the United States Military, the Greatest and Most Powerful Force in the World, and then served as my Deputy Surgeon General during my First Term,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on Thursday. “She is a STAR!” Before her deputy surgeon general position, she served as chief medical officer and director of health, safety and work-life for the U.S. Coast Guard, overseeing its health care system. She got her medical degree from Brown University School of Medicine and was a rear admiral in the U.S. Public Health Service Commissioned Corps. “It’s gotten applause from both Republicans and Democrats,” Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said about Trump's CDC pick at a House committee hearing on Thursday. “This new team is really going to be able to revolutionize CDC and get it back on track.” Trump also announced three additional names who will serve in key CDC roles: Sean Slovenski, former president of Walmart Health, as the CDC Deputy Director and Chief Operating Officer; Jennifer Shuford, commissioner of the Texas Department of State Health Services, as the CDC Deputy Director and Chief Medical Officer; and Sara Brenner, FDA Principal Deputy Commissioner, as Senior Counselor for Public Health to Kennedy. “These Highly Respected Doctors of Medicine have the knowledge, experience, and TOP degrees to restore the GOLD STANDARD OF SCIENCE at the CDC, which was an absolute disaster focused on ‘mandates’ under Sleepy Joe,” Trump wrote in the post. Jay Bhattacharya, the National Institutes of Health director, has served as CDC’s temporary head for months. Kennedy fired the last director, Susan Monarez, in August, after only a month on the job following a disagreement over vaccines. The nomination comes as the administration has tried to tamp down controversial vaccine policy changes and rhetoric ahead of the midterms and shift the health department's focus to Kennedy's nutrition agenda, which is considered more popular. If confirmed by the Senate, Schwartz will inherit an agency that has been shaken by an especially tumultuous year, including a shooting at the agency’s Atlanta headquarters last summer and multiple rounds of mass firings. The chaos — and lack of permanent leadership — has taken a heavy toll on CDC employees’ morale. The administration pulled the nomination of its original candidate, former Congressman Dave Weldon, in March 2025 after it became clear that he did not have the votes to advance out of committee. Weldon was an outspoken vaccine skeptic, a trait that helped tank his nomination. Schwartz, who isn't known for questioning vaccine safety, is expected to have an easier time winning Senate confirmation. But several of Kennedy’s most vocal supporters have taken issue with her. “Dr. Joseph Ladapo (@FLSurgeonGen) earned the right to be CDC Director with his courage and visionary leadership during Covid,” Toby Rogers, a MAHA activist and fellow at the Kennedy-aligned Brownstone Institute, wrote Wednesday on the social media platform X before Schwartz was officially selected. Rogers was referencing Florida Surgeon General Ladapo, who has said he wants to “end all vaccine mandates” for school-age children in the state. “Instead the White House is leaning toward Erica Schwartz who ordered the fraudulent PCR tests that were part of the Covid psyop,” Rogers continued. During the pandemic, Schwartz took on a role as the official physician ordering Covid-19 tests for drive-thru testing sites nationwide. Aaron Siri, a vaccine injury lawyer and managing partner of Siri & Glimstad, who's also worked as Kennedy's personal attorney, criticized Schwartz for her role in writing smallpox and anthrax vaccine mandates for some coast guard members during her time overseeing its health system. “This agency does not need another cheerleader for industry; it needs a regulator over industry,” Siri told POLITICO in a statement Thursday, prior to Trump's announcement. Jeff Hutt, who served as Kennedy’s national field director during his 2024 presidential campaign, told POLITICO he sees Kennedy as a “change agent.” Schwartz “is definitely not a change agent,” he added. He also pointed to the political reality: "You know, Bobby Kennedy only has so much say over what goes on in HHS.” Erica Schwartz is considered a more traditional pick for the CDC director role and does not have clear connections to the Make America Healthy Again movement. © Department of Health and Human Services via Wikimedia Commons ; ; ; ;
